stories.headline: Bajaj family enters health care with Nivara, bets on care beyond hospitals
stories.title: Bajaj family enters health care with Nivara, bets on care beyond hospitals
stories.summary: The Bajaj family is making a new bet on India's health care market, but it does not want to build just another hospital chain. With Nivara, its health care venture, the group is attempting to build an integrated health care platform that puts outpatient care, diagnostics, home health care and day surgery at the centre of its business, with hospitals forming one part of a larger ecosystem.At the formal launch of Bajaj Integrated Health Systems (BIHS) on November 19, Nirav Bajaj, managing director of the venture, outlined an approach that he said was rooted in the group's values of putting patients first and taking a long-term view of business building. The group believes that nearly 70 percent of health care problems can be addressed outside hospitals, and wants to build its network around this premise.The first step will be a medical centre at Amanora in Pune, which is scheduled to open next week. The facility will bring together diagnostics, medical testing, doctor consultations and physiotherapy under one roof. Patients will be able to access their medical reports in one place, while the centre will also have a dedicated play area for children.The Pune launch is significant for a family that has deep roots in the city. Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finance, two of the group's flagship businesses, are headquartered in Pune. The health care venture will initially use the city as a testing ground before taking its model to other markets. Nivara aims to establish a presence in six cities over 10 years.The next layer of the network will comprise home health care services and day-surgery centres. These centres will offer procedures and treatments such as dialysis, chemotherapy and endoscopy, among others, allowing patients to access services without having to visit a full-fledged hospital.Also Read: We are not focused solely on building large hospitals—we are building intelligent systems: Suneeta ReddyA 500-bed hospital is also planned in Pune, with construction expected to begin next year. It is likely to take three to four years to complete.The group had earlier announced an investment of ₹2,500 crore in its health care venture, which is being built as a continuum of care spanning neighbourhood medical centres, ambulatory facilities, home health care and multispecialty hospitals.One of the more interesting aspects of Nivara's proposed model is a subscription-based offering. Under this, customers would pay a monthly fee to cover their outpatient health care requirements. The company is also considering extending the offering to cover surgeries."We plan to add an option that allows subscription patients to be covered for everything, including surgeries," Bajaj said.The contours of this offering, including how it will be priced and whether the surgical component will involve an insurance arrangement, are yet to be spelt out. The distinction will be important in a market where outpatient expenses account for a significant part of household health care spending but are not adequately covered by traditional health insurance policies.The Bajaj group has an insurance business, but Bajaj clarified that it would operate independently of the health care venture. Nivara would deal with all insurance providers on an equal footing, with the relationship being conducted at arm's length.The opportunity is considerable. According to a March 2024 report by Bain & Company, India's overall health care market was valued at approximately $180 billion in FY23 and was projected to grow at around 12 percent annually to reach $320 billion by FY28. The report also estimated the health care innovation opportunity at $30 billion in FY23, with the potential to double to $60 billion by FY28.Importantly, consumer expectations are changing alongside the expansion of the market. Bain's research found that more than 70 percent of surveyed Indian consumers expected convenience and quality care to help them manage their health proactively. The use of digital health care applications, including telemedicine, e-pharmacy and wellness services, had increased by 20 to 100 percent during the pandemic. The report also pointed to the growing demand for integrated health care models that offer consumers a single point of access to multiple services.This is the space Nivara hopes to address by bringing different aspects of health care delivery under one umbrella.The entry comes at a time when India's organised hospital sector is expanding rapidly. Apollo Hospitals, one of the country's largest health care chains, reported a network of 78 hospitals and 10,970 beds in FY26, alongside more than 2,500 diagnostic centres. Max Healthcare, meanwhile, had an operational capacity of 5,518 beds at the end of September. Both companies have announced substantial capacity expansion plans.For Nivara, the proposition is that bringing services together can make health care easier to access and navigate, while also directing patients to the most appropriate and potentially less expensive setting for treatment.But building such a network will require more than capital. The company will need to attract medical talent, establish clinical credibility and ensure consistent standards across different formats of care. Its subscription model will also have to demonstrate that it can deliver value to patients while remaining commercially viable.For now, the Bajaj family is keeping its ambitions national, but its execution local. Pune will be the laboratory in which Nivara tests its integrated health care model before attempting to replicate it in other cities. The bigger test will be whether a business built around keeping patients out of hospitals as much as possible can emerge as a meaningful new player in India's increasingly competitive health care market.

stories.headline: An ode to love: The big, fat Indian wedding is back with a bang
stories.title: An ode to love: The big, fat Indian wedding is back with a bang
stories.summary: In August 2024, when US-based lawyer Sejal Makheja got engaged to her boyfriend Kbhi Mitter at Lake Como with just the family in attendance, it was the first of 27 events that culminated in a week of celebrations for their wedding in Dubai in February 2026. A full-blown engagement party—subsequently held at Legacy Castle in New York at the end of November 2024—with singer Mickey Singh performing (“a lot of people thought that was our wedding because we had almost 650 people,” says Makheja), was put together in two months. After Dubai was finalised in January as the venue for the marriage, the planning for the wedding took over.But the celebrations didn’t wait—the couple, their family and friends threw one event after another, showcasing the couple’s love story. They kept up the excitement leading up to the wedding with events such as a girls’ pre-wedding brunch and a surprise winery celebration.Also Read: Why luxury's biggest bet on India might be its costliest mistake“Each of our events had a unique theme,” says Makheja, most of them drawing on personal memories and meaningful moments in their story. “One of our favourite memories was a trip we took to Paris together. So for my husband’s Jaago night in New York, the theme was Mitter Mela Rouge, a nod to the Moulin Rouge show in Paris. The room was smoked red and there was an Eiffel Tower over the bar.” Mandaps are all about understated elegance and a serene atmosphere. A mandap at a wedding planned by DB Spaces (left); Lal Bagh mandap by Vandana Mohan’s The Wedding Design Company (right). Photo courtesy Sam & EktaThe wedding week themes were also based around their relationship. “We decided to make the wedding sort of a window into the relationship that brought us to the marriage, so each event was tailored around that,” she says.Also Read: Newer wedding destinations offer thrills and allure, from Baku to South AfricaFrom personal texts shared by a couple printed on napkins at the wedding to give a sneak peek into their story, and veils with motifs meaningful to the pair, to actors Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna’s wedding being an ode to their shared love of history and heritage, the big, fat Indian wedding is becoming more personal, reflecting the couples’ personalities. It has moved from massive impersonal flower arrangements to more intentional, sustainable décor. From having big names as entertainers to keeping guests engaged with experiences. And where true luxury is not a display of wealth and grandeur, but an understated elegance that puts the spotlight as much on the couple as on the guests.A generational shiftDuring the pandemic, weddings became intimate and smaller, but big weddings and celebrations returned with a vengeance after Covid-19. What has changed in the past few years, says Vandana Mohan, founder and creative director of wedding design and planning house The Wedding Design Company, is that things are being done with intent.“After Covid, it became ‘the bigger the better’. Everything came back in full force. But in the last few years, I’ve seen a huge change in intent. I think it’s also because youngsters today have not just excess but access to so much in life, there’s an overload of sensory things all around,” she says, adding that they are trying to make sense of things from all the madness and confusion, “and the only way they can do that is when they put themselves in the middle of it all”. Actors Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna’s (above) was an ode to their shared love of history and heritage. Photo courtesy House On The Clouds; RVR proTheir personality then takes centre stage. The trend is to do things with personalisation of traditions, culture and heritage, rather than just what is trending.It’s a thread that runs through weddings like Virosh’s (Vijay and Rashmika), arguably one of the biggest celebrity weddings of the year, to Makheja’s events and closer home, Mohan’s daughter Vedika’s wedding.Also Read: The new era of wedding shopping: Immersive, emotional and craft-centricFor Deverakonda and Mandanna’s wedding in February, recalls Priya Maganti, CEO and founder of RVR PRO, RVR Eventz & Design, who planned it, the brief was to look to history and heritage. “Whether it was the clothes, the jewellery or the decor, everything just flew in that concept. And it’s not like Vijay picked it up from another wedding. He just felt like if he is getting married, he wants it to be a certain way. And bring that rich Indian heritage and be organic,” she says, adding that the actor was clear—he didn’t want an extravagant wedding, but something meaningful.From antiques along pathways and descriptor scrolls to hunting down an antique knife for Deverakonda or drawing on old motifs for their jewellery, the attention was in the detail.With a mix of the traditional and the meaningful, Mohan’s daughter Vedika had a veil with motifs that held significance to the couple embroidered on it. “Chinese chopsticks, they love their Shih Tzu, so Shih Tzus, the beach, he’s a soccer freak, she’s into art, all of this was woven and embroidered on this huge veil, which now hangs in their house as a tapestry,” says Mohan.Makheja and Mitter’s love of travel also reflected in events like an Hermes beach collab haldi and a dholki event where a New York venue was transformed into the South of Italy. “Some of our favourite memories when we travel are of collaboration beach clubs, so we built one as our theme for our haldi, which was an Hermes collaboration with Kbhi and Sejal Beach Club,” recalls Makheja. The dholki night collab became Dolce & Gabbana. “So, everything was blue and yellow, there was lemon decor. It was an opportunity in the middle of winter to pretend you were in coastal Italy again,” she adds.Impersonal Pinterest boards for décor are passe. Today, when a couple picks decor, even if it means doing, say red, as a colour palette theme, there is some meaning to it. “Perhaps the bride’s favourite colour is red. So, when guests walk into these experiences, they’re not just seeing Pinterest boards, they’re seeing something with a story behind it,” says Maganti. While Makheja and Mitter’s wedding was a white backdrop contrasted with red outfits, the haldi was themed around a beach collab—an Hermes collaboration with Kbhi and Sejal Beach Club. Photo courtesy knotting bellsSpotlight on guest experienceAt a wedding organised by Dakshita Bhatla, founder and lead producer at DB and Spaces, a wedding planning and design firm, the couple did a wall of ‘Love Stories Before Us’. Wedding pictures of guests and close family were sourced and put up as a surprise and “every guest invited to the wedding got their wedding’s photo”, she recollects.Celebrations are increasingly not just about the couple but also about the guests who have come for a destination wedding. About having them experience something they wouldn’t on a regular basis. And about making the events experiential rather than having guests as mere spectators.Also Read: Raj Mantena: The low-profile tycoon behind the viral Udaipur weddingFor a wedding in Kochi in 2024, Mohan created a Sindhuri red mandap that looked like a temple, with muted red flowers all over, and when one walked in there were bells, incense and chanting. “More than the architecture and how beautiful it looked, what stayed with me was that when the wedding got over, 400 guests didn’t move from that space. They were immersed in it. When I asked somebody why they didn’t move, he said, ‘I’ve never been to a wedding site that is so serene. It’s a red mandap, but it’s so serene’, So, they just sat in that atmosphere, and we asked the bhajan singer if he would continue for another half an hour,” says Mohan.The shift towards experiential is everywhere—from food and drinks to events. Mohan reveals that for the Kochi wedding, she took over the parking lot and turned it into a sort of conservatory space that had many moods to it depending on the event and where guests could meander through. “We did lots of pop-ups everywhere where people were engaged. People get bored… I mean, after a while, how much mehndi and how much dancing can you do? So, we had these art corners, a wine tasting, a make your own food, pizza corner,” she says.Guest experience was also at the heart of Makheja’s dos. At the first event of the Dubai wedding, a red carpet put the spotlight on guests, turning them into stars in a city home to many Bollywood celebrities. At the Fire and Ice-themed reception (Makheja describes herself as fire and Mitter as ice—calm, cool, collected), guests made their way to the event from entrances based on the personalities they chose for themselves, and fire and liquid nitrogen cocktails added to the theme. The reception venue itself was kept a surprise with a single line instruction—wear comfortable shoes.Set up in the middle of the desert, it included camel rides for guests. “It was fun doing a reception in the desert. It was our way to let our guests leave feeling like they had seen all parts of Dubai—whether it was a beach club, the celebrity red carpet from the welcome event, the beach of our wedding day and the Middle Eastern element from the sangeet,” says Makheja.Couples today want to create experiences that are personal to them while ensuring their guests enjoy every moment, says Bhavnesh Sawhney, co-founder of FB Celebrations. “The choices are always intentional. Whether it’s the entertainment, music or overall experience, every element reflects the couple’s personality while also considering what their guests will genuinely appreciate.”Planners add that the question people are asking is ‘What will our guests remember? Is there something they couldn’t experience somewhere else?’ “So, there is a big shift from spectacle to experience. The shift is about exceptional hospitality, logistics, and curated performances and food experiences,” adds Damini Oberoi, founder and CEO, Q Events and Weddings.Speaking of going all out about creating a mood and experience, Ambika Gupta, founder and creative director at wedding design company The A-Cube Project, recollects a conversation with a UAE client who said they took their bathrooms seriously. Gupta usually decks up bathrooms with knickknacks and flowers at weddings, but this time, at the venue in London, they went on to do a complete set design for the restroom too, with a Bridgerton theme. It was unique, bespoke and became a talking point. “The kind of restroom we did, it could cover a mini function for someone in India. Even bridal photo shoots were done in that restroom, that’s how good it looked,” she says.True luxury, it would seem, is not in the tangibles, but in the intangibles. It’s about making sure you know how a particular guest likes their tea. It’s about not having guests rush through things, but adding one more day of comfort. It’s in the effort and thought that goes into not just what you plan for a guest but also how you make the guest feel. “Putting things together as a designer is a fine recipe between luxurious decor, food and sound to create an overall experience that does not overwhelm you but makes you feel like you belong,” says Punit Jasuja, founder of Punit Jasuja Productions-events & interiors. (Clockwise from above) A dinner set-up by Punit Jasuja with rustic cane chairs and warm woven pendant lighting; at a wedding by DB Spaces, napkins printed with messages by the couple provided a peek into their story; a Bridgerton themed restroom at a London wedding by The A-Cube Project. Photo courtesy Dinner setup: N Ram Pictures; Napkin image: The Blemish TalesWhere it’s goingAs costs go up, so do spends. According to WeddingSutra’s Annual Luxury & Destination Weddings Survey 2026, standard HNI wedding spends (excluding jewellery, clothing, travel and immediate family gifting) now hover between ₹1 crore and ₹5 crore. While for business families with a net worth of ₹300 crore to ₹400 crore, budgets have doubled from ₹2 crore to ₹4 crore pre-Covid to ₹5 crore to ₹10 crore in 2026.The shift towards personalisation and customisation have had a part to play. “Clients and their families expect top-notch service from the hospitality teams. And as weddings get more personalised, they become more manpower-intensive too,” says Parthip Thyagarajan, CEO of wedding media company WeddingSutra.com, adding that it is not uncommon sometimes for the crew numbers at a big wedding to be more than the guest size.Not just hospitality, the list of people connected with the recession-proof industry that encompasses everyone from carpenters and caterers to flower growers and fashion designers, too has grown. “There used to be just one panwala. Now the panwala has three specialisations. Then a photographer, videographer, candid and personal photographers for brides and grooms, content creators. It used to be one person for hair and makeup. Now there is somebody for makeup and styling,” says Mohan.But the major cost remains the venue, which accounts for 50 percent of a wedding spend at a destination (see box). And if it’s a royal wedding at Udaipur that is the ask, clearly, even HNI budgets are not enough. According to the WeddingSutra report, “Udaipur’s top-tier palace properties have reached unprecedented price points during peak season, effectively placing them out of reach for HNIs and rendering them almost exclusively accessible to ultra-HNIs.”And yet, true luxury is perhaps to not need to hire a venue at all. There are families, says Jasuja, that have huge estates all over the world and who can just throw a party in their garden. He adds that they have worked with clients where they have planted plants and flowers months in advance “so their garden is just what it needs to be—gorgeous and celebratory—without trying, understated and luxurious”.Sometimes, they need to add a few things, like a bridge or a platform, but most of the time, since the property is located at the bottom of a mountain or near a forest, there is not much to do. “Luxury is at your footsteps. We don’t need to create a set to project the taste or wealth, it’s just there,” says Jasuja.

From antiques along pathways and descriptor scrolls to hunting down an antique knife for Deverakonda or drawing on old motifs for their jewellery, the attention was in the detail.
With a mix of the traditional and the meaningful, Mohan’s daughter Vedika had a veil with motifs that held significance to the couple embroidered on it.

“Chinese chopsticks, they love their Shih Tzu, so Shih Tzus, the beach, he’s a soccer freak, she’s into art, all of this was woven and embroidered on this huge veil, which now hangs in their house as a tapestry,” says Mohan.
Makheja and Mitter’s love of travel also reflected in events like an Hermes beach collab haldi and a dholki event where a New York venue was transformed into the South of Italy.

“Some of our favourite memories when we travel are of collaboration beach clubs, so we built one as our theme for our haldi, which was an Hermes collaboration with Kbhi and Sejal Beach Club,” recalls Makheja.
The dholki night collab became Dolce & Gabbana.
“So, everything was blue and yellow, there was lemon decor.
It was an opportunity in the middle of winter to pretend you were in coastal Italy again,” she adds.
Impersonal Pinterest boards for décor are passe.
Today, when a couple picks decor, even if it means doing, say red, as a colour palette theme, there is some meaning to it.
“Perhaps the bride’s favourite colour is red.
So, when guests walk into these experiences, they’re not just seeing Pinterest boards, they’re seeing something with a story behind it,” says Maganti.
While Makheja and Mitter’s wedding was a white backdrop contrasted with red outfits, the haldi was themed around a beach collab—an Hermes collaboration with Kbhi and Sejal Beach Club.
Photo courtesy knotting bellsSpotlight on guest experience.
At a wedding organised by Dakshita Bhatla, founder and lead producer at DB and Spaces, a wedding planning and design firm, the couple did a wall of ‘Love Stories.
Before Us’.
Wedding pictures of guests and close family were sourced and put up as a surprise and “every guest invited to the wedding got their wedding’s photo”, she recollects.
Celebrations are increasingly not just about the couple but also about the guests who have come for a destination wedding.
About having them experience something they wouldn’t on a regular basis.
And about making the events experiential rather than having guests as mere spectators.
For a wedding in Kochi in 2024, Mohan created a Sindhuri red mandap that looked like a temple, with muted red flowers all over, and when one walked in there were bells, incense and chanting.
“More than the architecture and how beautiful it looked, what stayed with me was that when the wedding got over, 400 guests didn’t move from that space.
They were immersed in it.
When I asked somebody why they didn’t move, he said, ‘I’ve never been to a wedding site that is so serene.
It’s a red mandap, but it’s so serene’, So, they just sat in that atmosphere, and we asked the bhajan singer if he would continue for another half an hour,” says Mohan.
The shift towards experiential is everywhere—from food and drinks to events.

Mohan reveals that for the Kochi wedding, she took over the parking lot and turned it into a sort of conservatory space that had many moods to it depending on the event and where guests could meander through.
“We did lots of pop-ups everywhere where people were engaged.
People get bored… I mean, after a while, how much mehndi and how much dancing can you do?
So, we had these art corners, a wine tasting, a make your own food, pizza corner,” she says.
Guest experience was also at the heart of Makheja’s dos.
At the first event of the Dubai wedding, a red carpet put the spotlight on guests, turning them into stars in a city home to many Bollywood celebrities.

At the Fire and Ice-themed reception (Makheja describes herself as fire and Mitter as ice—calm, cool, collected), guests made their way to the event from entrances based on the personalities they chose for themselves, and fire and liquid nitrogen cocktails added to the theme.
The reception venue itself was kept a surprise with a single line instruction—wear comfortable shoes.
Set up in the middle of the desert, it included camel rides for guests.
“It was fun doing a reception in the desert.

It was our way to let our guests leave feeling like they had seen all parts of Dubai—whether it was a beach club, the celebrity red carpet from the welcome event, the beach of our wedding day and the Middle Eastern element from the sangeet,” says Makheja.
Couples today want to create experiences that are personal to them while ensuring their guests enjoy every moment, says Bhavnesh Sawhney, co-founder of FB Celebrations.
“The choices are always intentional.

Whether it’s the entertainment, music or overall experience, every element reflects the couple’s personality while also considering what their guests will genuinely appreciate.” Planners add that the question people are asking is ‘What will our guests remember?
Is there something they couldn’t experience somewhere else?’ “So, there is a big shift from spectacle to experience.
The shift is about exceptional hospitality, logistics, and curated performances and food experiences,” adds Damini Oberoi, founder and CEO, Q Events and Weddings.
Speaking of going all out about creating a mood and experience, Ambika Gupta, founder and creative director at wedding design company.
The A-Cube Project, recollects a conversation with a UAE client who said they took their bathrooms seriously.

Gupta usually decks up bathrooms with knickknacks and flowers at weddings, but this time, at the venue in London, they went on to do a complete set design for the restroom too, with a Bridgerton theme.
It was unique, bespoke and became a talking point.
“The kind of restroom we did, it could cover a mini function for someone in India.
Even bridal photo shoots were done in that restroom, that’s how good it looked,” she says.
True luxury, it would seem, is not in the tangibles, but in the intangibles.
It’s about making sure you know how a particular guest likes their tea.
It’s about not having guests rush through things, but adding one more day of comfort.
It’s in the effort and thought that goes into not just what you plan for a guest but also how you make the guest feel.

“Putting things together as a designer is a fine recipe between luxurious decor, food and sound to create an overall experience that does not overwhelm you but makes you feel like you belong,” says Punit Jasuja, founder of Punit Jasuja Productions-events & interiors.

(Clockwise from above) A dinner set-up by Punit Jasuja with rustic cane chairs and warm woven pendant lighting; at a wedding by DB Spaces, napkins printed with messages by the couple provided a peek into their story; a Bridgerton themed restroom at a London wedding by The A-Cube Project.
Photo courtesy Dinner setup: N Ram Pictures; Napkin image: The Blemish Tales.
Where it’s goingAs costs go up, so do spends.
According to Wedding.
Sutra’s Annual Luxury & Destination Weddings Survey 2026, standard HNI wedding spends (excluding jewellery, clothing, travel and immediate family gifting) now hover between ₹1 crore and ₹5 crore.
While for business families with a net worth of ₹300 crore to ₹400 crore, budgets have doubled from ₹2 crore to ₹4 crore pre-Covid to ₹5 crore to ₹10 crore in 2026.
The shift towards personalisation and customisation have had a part to play.
“Clients and their families expect top-notch service from the hospitality teams.

And as weddings get more personalised, they become more manpower-intensive too,” says Parthip Thyagarajan, CEO of wedding media company WeddingSutra.com, adding that it is not uncommon sometimes for the crew numbers at a big wedding to be more than the guest size.
Not just hospitality, the list of people connected with the recession-proof industry that encompasses everyone from carpenters and caterers to flower growers and fashion designers, too has grown.
“There used to be just one panwala.
Now the panwala has three specialisations.
Then a photographer, videographer, candid and personal photographers for brides and grooms, content creators.
It used to be one person for hair and makeup.
Now there is somebody for makeup and styling,” says Mohan.
But the major cost remains the venue, which accounts for 50 percent of a wedding spend at a destination (see box).
And if it’s a royal wedding at Udaipur that is the ask, clearly, even HNI budgets are not enough.

According to the WeddingSutra report, “Udaipur’s top-tier palace properties have reached unprecedented price points during peak season, effectively placing them out of reach for HNIs and rendering them almost exclusively accessible to ultra-HNIs.” And yet, true luxury is perhaps to not need to hire a venue at all.
There are families, says Jasuja, that have huge estates all over the world and who can just throw a party in their garden.

He adds that they have worked with clients where they have planted plants and flowers months in advance “so their garden is just what it needs to be—gorgeous and celebratory—without trying, understated and luxurious”.
Sometimes, they need to add a few things, like a bridge or a platform, but most of the time, since the property is located at the bottom of a mountain or near a forest, there is not much to do.
“Luxury is at your footsteps.
We don’t need to create a set to project the taste or wealth, it’s just there,” says Jasuja.

stories.title: Supreme Court upholds tribal land rights, quashes mining-linked acquisition in Odisha
stories.summary: Court says prior Gram Sabha consent was mandatory under the 2013 land acquisition law; sets aside acquisition for Dalmia Cement’s mining project in Sundargarh
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has stuck down the process of land acquisition for limestone mining in Odisha’s Sundargarh district after observing that the prior consent of the concerned Gram Sabha was mandatory for land acquisition in the Scheduled Areas, as per Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

Hearing the case of Bibol Toppo versus Odisha government and others, wherein acquisition of lands by the Odisha government for the purpose of mining by Dalmia Cements Bharat Limited was challenged, a Supreme Court bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Justice Satish Chandra Sharma ruled that the land cannot be acquired without prior consent of the Gram Sabha as per Section 41 of the 2013 Act.
“In finality we allow the writ petition and hold that the land acquisition in question is unsustainable.
The acquisition, along with the relevant notifications and orders is hereby set aside,” Supreme Court judges ruled.

The appellants were residents of Kukuda, Bihabandha and Lanjiberna villages in Odisha’s Sundargarh district, challenging land acquisition initiated by the State government for Dalmia Cement Bharat Limited.
The State Government had granted a mining lease to the company for conducting mining operations over an area of 893.55 Ha.
The company held the mining lease, extended until February 2040, but sought to acquire 273.57 hectares of the land across the three villages to obtain surface rights required for mining operations.
The land acquisition was challenged in Orissa High Court.
The court had held that the requirement of prior consent did not apply as it was an acquisition by the State, as the State was being clothed with the right, title or interest in the land.

The court had further held that even if the requirement of obtaining prior consent of 80% land owners was applicable, the process of taking consent ought to be a continuing process which takes place through the various stages of the acquisition proceedings.
On the basis of this position, the court had acknowledged that a total 535 affected persons have given their consent in Form J as per Odisha Rules of 2013 Act, which satisfies the legal requirement.
Petitioner Mr. Toppo, however, submitted that the provisions of prior consent are mandatory and not directory.

stories.title: Karnataka Cabinet clears projects worth ₹4,000 crore for Bengaluru city, approves ₹10,250 crore for development of nine State Highways
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet clears' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Karnataka government on Thursday approved projects worth over ₹4,000 crore for Bengaluru city, while also approving development of nine State Highways at a cost of around ₹10,250 crore.
The Cabinet approved distribution of 5 lakh sites as part of Bhoo Guarantee by December or January for which 24,000 acres of government land has been identified.

The Cabinet approved suspension and investigation to be instituted by the Governor against Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) member B.V. Geetha, who has been arrested by the Special Investigation Team in connection with the recruitment scam.

About 730-km stretch of road on nine State Highways in Mysuru, Mandya, Chamarajanagar, Kodagu, Hassan, Bengaluru South, Vijayapura, Kalaburagi, Belagavi, Bagalkot, Koppal, and Gadag district will be developed at a cost of around ₹10,252 crore.
Approval was given to deploy 2,000 electric buses on gross cost contract scheme at a cost of ₹1,700 crore, including World Bank assistance of ₹1,400 crore.

While 1,000 buses would be provided to Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, 500 buses each will be provided to Kittur Rani Chennamma Road Transport Corporation and Kalyana Karnataka Road Transport Corporation.
Among the projects approved for Bengaluru are the white-topping of 130 km stretch of 88 roads in the city at a cost ₹2,321 crore by Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure Ltd.
and elevating the outer ring road stretch between Silk Board Junction and K.R. Puram Metro Station to global standards at a revised cost of ₹486 crore.

Other Cabinet decisions on Thursday included approval of purchase and distribution of laptops at a cost of ₹50,000 each to 5,000 students belonging to minority communities studying in B.E. and BCA courses.

The Cabinet did not agree to the proposal by Minority Welfare, Haj and Wakf Department for direct cash transfers to students, and instead directed the department to purchase the laptops for distribution.

It also agreed waive interest amount of ₹236.06 crore on repayment of principal by beneficiaries for loans sanctioned by seven development corporations under Backward Classes Welfare Department between 2013 and 2021 under a one-time payment scheme.
Beneficiaries have in total defaulted payment of ₹577 crore, Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara said in the post Cabinet briefing.

stories.headline: Supreme Court directs verification, remedial measures against bogus Form-7s in Delhi’s Mustafabad
stories.title: Supreme Court directs verification, remedial measures against bogus Form-7s in Delhi’s Mustafabad
stories.summary: The petition drew attention to an investigation by The Hindu, which reported that 28 electors against whom deletion applications had been submitted were physically traced at the addresses at which they were enrolled
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (November 19, 2026) directed authorities to verify allegations that fabricated Form-7s were filed to delete genuine voters from electoral rolls in Delhi’s Mustafabad Assembly Constituency during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and take all remedial measures.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant even urged Congress leader Ali Mehdi, represented by advocate Shariq Ahmed, to approach the jurisdictional magistrate if the police have refused to register an FIR on his complaint about fabrication and forgery.
The order was passed on Mr. Mehdi’s plea that a “substantial” number of ghost Form-7s seeking deletion of voters had been detected, and that a crisis of electoral integrity is brewing.

The writ petition said that voters whose names were put forward for deletion on the grounds of death, absence, or permanent shifting were found to be very much alive, present, and residing at their recorded addresses on the electoral roll.
The persons in whose names Form-7s had been filed for deletion of these voters deny having filed or signed on the applications.
“The integrity of an electoral roll is compromised not only when an ineligible name remains upon it.
It is equally compromised when an eligible elector is removed from it on a fact which never existed or upon an objection which the supposed objector never made.
The present record discloses the latter danger in its stark form,” the writ petition said.
It said persons declared dead were alive, while persons said to have shifted were found at home.
Of the 37 applications examined by electoral authorities, 36 were found to be false or fabricated.
“The existence of a genuine objector and the existence of a genuine ground for deletion — In Mustafabad, both are under serious doubt at the same time,” Mr. Ahmed submitted.

Section 22 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 requires the Electoral Registration Officer to be satisfied, after proper verification of the facts, before an entry can be corrected or deleted.

article_sentences: A Delhi court has sought a detailed account of the police action on the complaint filed by a journalist who accused Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Vivek Bhagat of groping her while she was covering the detention of student leader Neha Bora at Jantar Mantar on October 3.
On November 16, the Delhi.

Police told the Supreme Court that sexual assault cases by three women journalists during the anti-SIR protests in the Capital in October were ‘closed’, while in a fourth case, no video evidence was found to warrant further proceedings.

In an order dated November 3, accessed by The Hindu, Judicial Magistrate First Class Kautuk Bhardwaj of the Patiala House Courts directed the Station House Officer (SHO) concerned to submit an action taken report (ATR), answering five specific questions about the complaint and the subsequent police inquiry.
The Court asked the SHO to state whether the complaint had been received at the police station and, if so, what action had been taken.
It also sought details on whether the investigation or inquiry established the commission of any cognisable offence against the accused and whether any action followed.
If an FIR had been registered, the police were asked to provide its status and the progress of the investigation.
If no cognisable offence had been made out, the SHO was required to clarify whether the complainant had been informed of the decision.
The Court directed that the response be filed “point-wise”, addressing each of its queries and detailing the action taken on the complaint before the complainant approached the Court.
The Court also directed the SHO to take all necessary steps within three days of receiving the order to preserve the relevant CCTV footage and other digital evidence, including body-camera footage.
The compliance report on the preservation of the evidence is to be filed within a week.
The matter is listed for December 1 for the filing of the ATR.

stories.title: Maharashtra Entertainment Duty Act | Business-To-Business Trade Exhibitions Liable To Duty If Entry Is Paid : Supreme Court
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has held that business-to-business trade exhibitions can fall within the definition of “entertainment” under the Maharashtra Entertainment Duty Act, 1923, if persons are admitted to them upon payment.

Dismissing an appeal by the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC), the Court upheld the levy of entertainment duty on its annual India International Jewellery Show (IIJS) and IIJS Signature exhibitions organised in Mumbai.
“…we notice that, in the case at hand, entry into the IIJS and IIJS Signature is on payment.
Further, exhibitions showcase the merchandise of the participating traders.
The entry is on payment, and upon entry, even if it is a business-to-business transaction, the same cannot be taken away from the definition of “entertainment” under the Act, 1923.

The requirement of filling up the form for entry can be for more than one purpose, including security reasons, and cannot be taken advantage of to wriggle out of an otherwise plain and simple reading of “entertainment” in Section 2(a) of the Act, 1923.”, observed a bench of Justice SVN Bhatti and Justice NV Anjaria.

The Appellant-Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council organises annual exhibitions titled India International Jewellery Show (“IIJS”) and “IIJS Signature”, which provide a platform for interaction among exporters, other jewellers of the country, and foreign buyers visiting the show.

stories.headline: Budgam meat seizure: FDA directs Railways to ensure licensed FBOs transport perishable food commodities under prescribed conditions
stories.title: Budgam meat seizure: FDA directs Railways to ensure licensed FBOs transport perishable food commodities under prescribed conditions
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 19: The Food and Drugs Administration (FDA), Jammu and Kashmir, has issued an advisory to railway authorities, directing that highly perishable food commodities be transported only through duly licensed Food Business Operators (FBOs) and under prescribed temperature-controlled conditions, with proper declarations and documentation. The advisory follows the seizure and destruction of around 1,600 kg of frozen meat at Budgam Railway Station, where the consignment was allegedly transported through the railway parcel service by misrepresenting it as general goods. In a press statement, the FDA said the action was taken after receiving specific information from Railway Police authorities. The frozen meat was found to have been transported without proper temperature-control arrangements to maintain the required frozen conditions. A preliminary investigation revealed that the consignment originated from M/s Al Nida Foods, Ghazipur, Delhi, and was intended for Ayaan Manzoor, a resident of Bemina, Srinagar, through M/s Tultrav Courier Agency, Bemina. The consignment had reportedly been booked under the general parcel category without disclosing the actual nature of the commodity, apparently to circumvent the prescribed requirements for transporting highly perishable food products under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The FDA said inspection of the consignment and accompanying documents revealed discrepancies in the description of the commodity and violations of labelling norms, attracting provisions of Sections 53 and 61 of the Act. It was also found that the transporter and intended recipient did not possess the mandatory FSSAI licences, attracting penal provisions under Section 63. Considering the potential threat to public health, the entire consignment was seized and destroyed through the Municipal Committee, Budgam, at a designated disposal site. The department said notices had been issued to the concerned persons and entities, while further legal proceedings were being initiated under the relevant provisions of the Act. The FDA also referred to similar enforcement actions undertaken during 2025, when frozen meat and meat products were seized from five establishments across Srinagar. These included 1,200 kg from M/s Sunshine Industries, Zakura; 500 kg from M/s Al-Taqwa, Lasjan; 1,400 kg from M/s M.M. Foods, Haji Bagh, HMT; 420 kg from M/s Niyaz Ahmad Kawa, Aali Kadal; and 520 kg from M/s Al-Azeem Enterprises, Manderbagh. Following these seizures, legal proceedings were initiated against the respective Food Business Operators. The Court of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar, acting as the Adjudicating Officer, imposed penalties of Rs 4 lakh, Rs 5 lakh, Rs 4.40 lakh, Rs 1.25 lakh and Rs 17,500, respectively. The department further stated that two samples collected from the establishments were examined by the ICAR-National Meat Research Institute, Hyderabad, and identified as buffalo meat. To prevent such violations, the FDA had issued a prohibitory order on October 3, 2025, restricting the transportation, storage and sale of frozen food products without prescribed temperature-control arrangements and mandatory labelling under the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020. Meanwhile, the department said it had conducted 12,778 inspections across Jammu and Kashmir during the financial year 2026-27, lifting 7,266 enforcement samples and 2,857 surveillance samples for analysis through NABL-accredited laboratories. During the same period, 533 cases were instituted and 619 cases adjudicated, resulting in penalties amounting to Rs 1,00,42,231 under various provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act. Following the Budgam incident, FDA field teams intensified enforcement activities, conducting 364 inspections, suspending nine FSSAI licences or registrations, issuing 21 improvement notices and recommending 31 cases for adjudication. More than 19 cases were also compounded under Section 69 of the Act. The FDA also said that funding-related issues concerning manpower and laboratory requirements had been resolved after the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), Government of India, approved the action plan submitted by the department for the financial years 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29. The approval will facilitate the recruitment of laboratory analysts, microbiologists, drivers and other personnel, besides procurement of chemicals, consumables and glassware for the government food laboratories in Srinagar and Jammu. The procurement process for laboratory manpower through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal has reached its final stage, while the procurement of certified reference materials, chemicals and glassware is expected to be completed within two weeks, the department said. Annual maintenance contracts for high-end laboratory equipment have also been executed with the respective original equipment manufacturers, while method validation is underway. Contracts for hiring drivers and laboratory analysts for Mobile Food Testing Vans have also been finalised, with personnel being deployed for operational activities. The department said it was working to expand the NABL-accredited testing scope of the government food laboratories to 2,500 parameters by January 2027 and 3,500 parameters by March 2027. Additional NABL-accredited and FSSAI-recognised laboratories are also being empanelled to strengthen testing capacity and ensure timely analysis of enforcement and surveillance samples. The FDA said it would continue intensified surveillance and enforcement to ensure compliance with food safety standards and appealed to consumers to share specific information about violations with the department for timely action.
